entries.title: Visitors explore the Obama Presidential Center museum on opening day
entries.summary: <p>Some were wowed by the feeling of sitting behind the desk in the Oval Office replica.</p><p>One visitor thought of all the people who helped build the place — because she's married to one of them.</p><p>And still others were just overwhelmed by remembering what the election of the first Black president meant to them, and to the country,</p><p>That's just a few of the thoughts from the visitors lucky enough to score much-coveted tickets to the museum of the Obama Presidential Center on its grand opening.</p><p>They were among thousands of visitors from across the country who packed nearly every corner of the campus in Jackson Park Friday to celebrate a place and a president on Juneteenth.</p><h3>Delores Mcclendon, 45, Englewood</h3><p>Delores Mcclendon spent hours touring the museum, but one installation in particular gave her the chance to relive one of the most significant moments not only of her own life, but for many others as well.</p><p>Mcclendon said the exhibit that stood out most was a video replaying the day former President Barack Obama won the 2008 presidential election.</p><p>“I remember that night, sitting there watching with my family,” said Mcclendon. “We were all shedding tears as he was getting closer and closer to winning. We were rejoicing.”</p><p>But before he became president, Obama was her neighbor, she said.</p><p>“He's from Chicago and that's the most exciting thing to me,” said Mcclendon. “To know that somebody that came up in the same community, and made it this far, made such a great impact in our nation, is incredible.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" </div><p></p><h3>Janice Murdock, 62, Auburn Gresham </h3><h3></h3><p>As Janice Murdock walked through the replica of the Oval Office, she said she couldn’t help but reflect on how far Black Americans have come.</p><p>“It’s overwhelming,” she said. “To be able to sit in the seat that [Barack Obama] sat in is awe-inspiring.”</p><p>The moment felt even more meaningful as opening day coincided with Juneteenth, a holiday commemorating emancipation, and one giving Black Americans an opportunity to celebrate freedom.</p><p>Murdock said the museum is a reflection of everything Obama was able to accomplish.</p><p>“He continues to give us so much hope,” said Murdock. “He set a standard that we so long looked for.”</p><h3>Verena Jimenez, 33, West Lawn</h3><h3></h3><p>Verena Jimenez said she enjoyed walking through the museum and taking in the artwork, but what made the experience especially meaningful was knowing her husband played a role in building a piece of history.</p><p> Victor Guevara, was among the construction workers who helped build the Obama Presidential Center. His name is engraved on the Worker Appreciation Wall, a permanent installation honoring the thousands of people who worked on the project.</p><p>Guevara smiled shyly as his wife spoke about his accomplishment.</p><p>“It’s been a great experience,” he said.</p><p>He and his wife brought their children to the museum on opening day, where Jimenez said she was grateful to get a glimpse at Obama’s legacy.</p><p>“He is one of the greatest presidents this country has ever seen,” she said. “He’s impacted our family and thousands of other people.”</p><div class="Enhancement" museum.</p><p>Armstead said Michelle Obama is an inspiration for many Black women, showing what can be achieved.</p><p>“She is a beautiful person,” said Armstead. “She helped create all of this so she deserves to also be celebrated.”</p><p>Armstead called the Obamas “icons” and said she was grateful to have had the opportunity to visit the museum.</p><p>“They are world leaders,” she said. “They are but there was one thing on display that caught her eye.</p><p>Yarbrough said she loved seeing a copy of the welcome letter George W. Bush wrote for Obama when he became the 44th president of the United States.</p><p>The letter was displayed inside an open drawer in the president's desk.</p><p>“To be able to read those words was amazing,” she said. “He was the first Black president, and it was important to see he was embraced by others.”</p><p>Yarbrough said Obama’s leadership was “legendary” and that what he accomplished during his presidency changed the country “for the better.”<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox say longtime shortstop Jacob Gonzalez catching on fast at first
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — What makes the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ playoff push unique is the fact that they’re doing it with players lacking major-league experience. And some of them aren’t just lacking that — they’re lacking it at the position they’re playing.</p><p>Case in point: Jacob Gonzalez.</p><p>The Sox called up Gonzalez with the intention of playing him at first base after Munetaka Murakami strained his right hamstring May 29, even though Gonzalez, primarily a shortstop, had started only five games there in his college and minor-league careers. He forced his way onto the roster with 19 home runs in 52 games at Triple-A Charlotte this season.</p><p>“He’s here to play first base for us,” Venable said days after Gonzalez’s call-up. “We’re going to support him.”</p><p>That they are.</p><p>“That’s where it gets lost with guys that play in the middle or even just on the left side of the infield,” Sox third-base and infield coach Justin Jirschele told the Sun-Times. “Go over to first base, and it’ll be easy. But it’s not. There’s a lot of nuance to it.”</p><p>Though Gonzalez has had a couple of mental miscues, he’s handling the physical aspects of the position well. In fact, according to the website The Fielding Bible, Gonzalez has a defensive runs saved of plus-two, meaning he’s above average (average is zero).</p><p>“The amount of runs he’s saved, the amount of double plays he’s started, the amount of picks he’s had in the dirt, overall, he’s been really, really good,” Jirschele said. “Especially for how new he is there.</p><p>“He’s working on his backhand. And you have to remember, he’s used to using a [smaller] glove, and now it’s damn near double. Yeah, it’s a bigger glove to catch throws, but fielding ground balls, it’s a much different feel.”</p><p>His two blunders were costly. On June 2 against the Twins, he moved to field a ball bunted back to pitcher Davis Martin, putting him out of position to take Martin’s throw. On Tuesday against the Yankees, he thought a ball was headed to the outfield, so he moved toward the mound to be the cut-off man. When second baseman Chase Meidroth fielded it, he had no one to throw to.</p><p>Gonzalez’s lesson: Go to the base first.</p><p>“The game’s always the best teacher for all of us,” Jirschele said. “We’re going to make mistakes; we learn from them. That’s exactly what I told him [Wednesday]. ‘I bet you that doesn’t happen again because you’re going to learn from that.’ ”</p><p>Where Gonzalez’s experience as a shortstop comes in handy is when he’s manning the right side of the infield seemingly alone with a right-handed hitter at the plate.</p><p>“If you watch where he’s playing and how aggressive he is on right-handed hitters, he’s almost halfway to second base,” Jirschele said. “But he’s comfortable enough to play there. It doesn’t happen a ton, but just optically, it takes away righties from feeling comfortable. It speaks volumes to how much he’s grown there in such a short period of time.”</p><p>Though Gonzalez has started just once this week, it has nothing to do with his play at first and everything to do with matchups. The Sox have faced three lefties, putting the left-handed-hitting Gonzalez on the bench. He’ll be in the lineup Saturday, when the Tigers start right-hander Troy Melton. That’s another issue for Gonzalez, who’s hitless in his last seven games.</p><p>But in the field, maybe we’ll see something else Gonzalez has learned. This much is certain: The Sox like what they’re seeing.</p><p>“All in all, it’s just a new position that he’s extremely young in,” Jirschele said. “He’s young in general, but extremely young at first base. We’re extremely happy with how he’s taken to it.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: Cubs' offense erupts for 16 runs, including seven-run first inning
entries.summary: <p>The Cubs would like to believe they're getting back to being their old, offensive selves.</p><p> </p><p>They hit the Toronto Blue Jays and veteran starter Kevin Gausman with seven runs in the first inning on Friday at Wrigley Field and just kept pouring it on in a 16-2 win.</p><p> </p><p>Carson Kelly provided the big blow in the early outburst —  his second career grand slam — off Gausman’s first pitch to him, a down-the-middle slider. </p><p> </p><p>Seiya Suzuki’s double to the right field corner had already given the North Siders a 2-0 lead. Then Kelly’s drive sailed 428-feet, landed just under the left-field video board and made it it 6-0.</p><p> </p><p>Add three more singles and the Cubs tied their season-high with seven runs in a frame.  </p><p></p><p>The rally was enough for the Cubs to win a second straight game and for the sixth time in eight.  Starter Ben Brown went on cruise control, throwing 51 of 72 pitches for strikes through six innings, walking none. The right-hander allowed just two runs on four hits to win his third straight decision</p><p> </p><p>It also was the third time the North Siders scored three runs in inning this season.  It also was the second time in<i> two games</i>, following a seven-run second inning in an 8-6 win at Colorado on Wednesday.</p><p> </p><p>“Right from the get-go, guys put pressure on them," said Kelly, who finished with career-high six RBIs. "It was get it to the next guy, continued to get it to the next guy. It was awesome.”</p><p> </p><p>The Cubs finished with 18 hits against defending the AL champs in this one. This is a Cubs squad that piled up runs early in the season during two 10-game winning streaks that book-ended a 20-3 run.</p><p> </p><p>Gausman issued four walks, along with yielding five hits in the first to set up the Cubs big inning as they sent 12 men to the plate. Gausman said he was wilder than usual – he entered having issued just 16 passes in 87 innings </p><p></p><p>“I wish I could point to something,” Gausman said. "The walks more than anything. That’s not normally me.”</p><p> </p><p>Meanwhile,the The Cubs were prudent.</p><p> </p><p>We did a good job against him to get that rally moving,” manager Craig Counsell said. "Obviously we got a huge hit from Carson, but we made (Gausman) come in the zone and laid off the splitter down and off the slider away to the righties and that’s important."</p><p> </p><p>Lead-off man Pete Crow-Armstrong continued to sizzle at the plate. The dynamic center fielder had three singles, an RBI and walked twice to extend his career-high on-base streak to 22 games, He’s batting .409 during the stretch.</p><p> </p><p>The free-swinging slugger is up to 27 walks in 76 games his season. He had 29 for all for 2025.</p><p> </p><p>“Today was the definition of who we are,” Crow-Armstrong said. "Drawing walks agaist a guys who doesn’t walk many, mixed with hits and homers.. or a homer. </p><p> </p><p>"That’s exactly who we are. We put ourselves in really good opportunities today to hit with guys guys on.  Contrary to recently, we made the most of those opportunities really well. Today was just a really good example of who this team is."</p><p></p><p>The Cubs accepted a total of 11 walks in this one from seven pitchers, including Toronto outfielder Miles Straw who mopped up for the final four outs.</p><p></p><p>The Cubs added four more runs in the sixth and five in the seventh. Seiya Suzuki and Nico Hoerner each had a double among three hits.</p><p> </p><p>The biggest, most emotional knock was a triple from Justin Dean, a 29-year-old who had been called up from Triple-A Iowa before the game and replaced Crow-Armstrong in center in the seventh.  The journeyman’s first major league hit drove in three runs.</p><p> </p><p>Dean sliced a drive of right-handed submariner Tyler Rogers beyond Jesus Sanchez to the right field corrner, then raced to third.  Dean appeared in 18 games with the Dodgers last season, but had only two at-bats has he was used in pinch-hitting and defensive replacement roles after a mix of 10 seasons in the minors, Mexico and college ball.<br></p>
